description: Matched-set prompt-efficacy dataset: 25 effects x 5 knowledge tiers. L3 is verbatim from prompts.json (anchors the committed 84% first-try baseline). Tier rules: L4 must name algorithm/topology + at least one numeric range; L3 = informed producer (effect + parameter names); L2 = functional lay description, no parameter jargon; L1 = sensory metaphor only, no effect-category or parameter names; L0 = artist/song/gear reference only, no mechanical description. expected_primitives is an ANY-OF substring list used by score_efficacy.py as a coarse semantic heuristic (weak for the trivial category by design).

tiers.L4: A stereo gain utility: single gain parameter in decibels, range -60 to +12 dB, default 0 dB, 0.1 dB steps, converted dB-to-linear and applied equally to both channels.
tiers.L3: a simple stereo gain control with a dB slider
tiers.L2: a simple volume knob to make my track louder or quieter
tiers.L1: let me push a sound forward or fade it back until it almost disappears
tiers.L0: just the channel volume fader from an SSL mixing console

tiers.L4: A stereo mute utility: one boolean checkbox parameter; when engaged the output is hard-muted (gain 0), when off audio passes unchanged; no other controls.
tiers.L3: a mute toggle with one boolean parameter
tiers.L2: an on/off switch that silences my track completely when I flip it
tiers.L1: a kill switch - one press and everything goes dead quiet, press again and it's all back
tiers.L0: the cut button DJs slam on a Pioneer mixer to drop a channel out

tiers.L4: A mono-to-stereo converter: one input channel duplicated to left and right outputs at unity gain (a 1-to-2 signal split); no parameters required.
tiers.L3: a mono-to-stereo converter that duplicates the channel
tiers.L2: take my mono recording and make it come out of both speakers
tiers.L1: my sound only lives in one ear - make it fill both sides evenly
tiers.L0: what a Y-split cable does to a mono bass signal in a stereo session

tiers.L4: A DC-blocking filter: first-order pole-zero highpass with cutoff around 10-20 Hz that removes DC offset while leaving the audible band untouched; stereo, no parameters needed.
tiers.L3: a DC blocker that removes low-frequency offset
tiers.L2: something that cleans up the inaudible low rumble that makes my waveform sit off-center
tiers.L1: my waveform is lopsided and pushes the speakers without making any sound - fix that
tiers.L0: the thing audio interfaces do so a wonky synth signal doesn't slowly shove your speaker cones

tiers.L4: A polarity inverter: multiplies the signal by -1, with a bypass checkbox that toggles between inverted and unprocessed signal; stereo.
tiers.L3: a polarity inverter with a bypass switch
tiers.L2: a switch that flips my audio's waveform upside down, with a way to turn it off
tiers.L1: when I layer my two mics the sound goes thin and hollow - give me the switch that fixes that
tiers.L0: the little Ø button on every mixing console channel strip

tiers.L4: A stereo resonant low-pass filter: 24 dB/oct ladder-style response, cutoff 20 Hz-20 kHz with exponential taper defaulting to 1 kHz, resonance Q 0.5-10, and gentle saturation for analog character.
tiers.L3: a warm analog-style low-pass filter with cutoff and resonance
tiers.L2: something that makes my sound darker and rounder, with one knob for how dark and another that makes it squelch when turned up
tiers.L1: make my synth sound warm and muffled, like it's playing from another room behind a wall
tiers.L0: the squelchy sweep sound from Daft Punk's 'Da Funk'

tiers.L4: A stereo high-pass filter: 2nd-order Butterworth response (12 dB/oct), cutoff 20 Hz-2 kHz with exponential taper, default 100 Hz.
tiers.L3: a high-pass filter with a gentle 12dB per octave slope
tiers.L2: a tool that thins out the boomy low end so only the crisp top part of my sound is left
tiers.L1: make it sound like it's coming out of a tiny phone speaker, all the weight gone
tiers.L0: the button engineers press on every vocal channel of a mixing desk

tiers.L4: A stereo band-pass filter: 2nd-order resonant design, center frequency 100 Hz-8 kHz with exponential taper defaulting to 1 kHz, Q adjustable 0.5-20.
tiers.L3: a band-pass filter with adjustable center frequency and Q
tiers.L2: keep just one narrow slice of my sound and cut everything above and below it, with knobs for where the slice sits and how narrow it is
tiers.L1: make my track sound like it's squeezed through a walkie-talkie
tiers.L0: the telephone-voice sound on Julian Casablancas' vocals on early Strokes records

tiers.L4: A stereo notch filter tuned for hum removal: center frequency 40-120 Hz defaulting to 60 Hz, adjustable width (Q 1-50), deep attenuation at the center frequency.
tiers.L3: a notch filter for removing 60Hz hum, with a width control
tiers.L2: something that surgically removes an annoying electrical buzz from my recording without changing how the rest sounds, plus a control for how wide the cut is
tiers.L1: my recording has a constant low mosquito-drone underneath everything - carve just that out and leave the rest alone
tiers.L0: what studio engineers use to kill the ground-loop buzz from a guitar amp plugged into a bad outlet

tiers.L4: A stereo high-shelf EQ: corner frequency 2-16 kHz defaulting to 8 kHz, shelf gain -12 to +12 dB, gentle slope suitable for adding 'air' to vocals.
tiers.L3: a high-shelf filter for adding air to vocals
tiers.L2: a brightness knob that adds sparkle to the top of my vocal, or dulls it down if I turn it the other way
tiers.L1: make my singer sound expensive - like the recording suddenly has fresh air and light around it
tiers.L0: the silky top-end lift mastering engineers get from a Pultec on the vocal bus

tiers.L4: A stereo delay: delay time 1-2000 ms defaulting to 350 ms, feedback 0-95%, dry/wet mix 0-100%, using an interpolated delay line for click-free time changes.
tiers.L3: a stereo delay with time, feedback, and dry/wet
tiers.L2: an echo effect with knobs for how far apart the echoes are, how many times they repeat, and how loud they are next to the original
tiers.L1: make my guitar answer itself, with trailing copies fading off into the distance
tiers.L0: the dotted-eighth echo The Edge uses on 'Where the Streets Have No Name'

tiers.L4: A ping-pong delay: cross-fed left/right delay lines so successive echoes alternate channels strictly L-R-L, delay time 50-1500 ms, feedback 0-90%, dry/wet mix.
tiers.L3: a ping-pong delay that bounces between left and right
tiers.L2: an echo that bounces back and forth between my left and right speakers as it fades
tiers.L1: throw my sound across the room - it should ricochet from one side to the other while it dies away
tiers.L0: the bouncing stereo echo all over Pink Floyd's 'One of These Days'

tiers.L4: A stereo chorus: modulated delay of 5-30 ms, LFO rate 0.1-5 Hz defaulting to 0.8 Hz, depth 0-100%, equal-power dry/wet mix, with LFO phase offset between channels for width.
tiers.L3: a subtle chorus effect with rate and depth
tiers.L2: an effect that makes one instrument sound like several playing the same part slightly apart, with knobs for how fast and how strong the shimmer is
tiers.L1: make my clean guitar sound wide, watery and dreamy, like it's gently swaying underwater
tiers.L0: the glassy warble on Kurt Cobain's guitar in 'Come as You Are'

tiers.L4: A stereo flanger: short modulated delay 0.5-10 ms swept by a 0.05-2 Hz LFO, feedback -0.95 to +0.95 for tape-style resonance, dry/wet mix.
tiers.L3: a tape-style flanger with feedback
tiers.L2: a whooshing jet-plane sweep that slowly moves up and down over my sound, with a control for how intense the swirl gets
tiers.L1: make my drums feel like they're being pulled through a wind tunnel that slowly breathes
tiers.L0: the psychedelic swooshing sweep on Small Faces' 'Itchycoo Park'

tiers.L4: A plate-style reverb: dense early diffusion feeding an allpass/feedback-delay network, decay time 0.5-8 s, high-frequency damping control, dry/wet mix, stereo output.
tiers.L3: a simple plate reverb with decay time and damping
tiers.L2: a smooth wash that makes my vocal sound like it's in a big room, with knobs for how long the tail lasts and how dark it gets
tiers.L1: give my voice a halo - a soft silver shimmer that hangs in the air after every word
tiers.L0: the lush metal-plate vocal reverb on every 1960s Abbey Road record

tiers.L4: A stereo feed-forward compressor: threshold -60 to 0 dB, ratio 1:1 to 20:1, attack 0.1-100 ms, release 10-1000 ms, with makeup gain.
tiers.L3: a compressor with threshold, ratio, attack, and release
tiers.L2: something that evens out my track's volume - it catches the loud hits and lifts the quiet parts so everything sits together
tiers.L1: glue my mix so it feels dense and controlled, like a firm hand keeping every sound in its place
tiers.L0: that punchy 'everything glued together' drum sound on Dr. Dre records

tiers.L4: A brick-wall limiter for mastering: ceiling -20 to 0 dBFS defaulting to -0.3 dBFS, sub-millisecond attack, release 10-500 ms; output must never exceed the ceiling.
tiers.L3: a brick-wall limiter for mastering
tiers.L2: a safety wall that stops my song from ever going over a set loudness, no matter how hard I push into it
tiers.L1: make my track slam as loud as it can possibly go without ever cracking apart
tiers.L0: the loudness-war sound of a 2000s mastered CD like 'Californication'

tiers.L4: A noise gate: threshold -80 to 0 dB, hold time 0-500 ms, fast attack and moderate release, closing to silence whenever the input falls below threshold.
tiers.L3: a noise gate with threshold and hold time
tiers.L2: something that automatically mutes my mic in the gaps between phrases so you can't hear the background hiss
tiers.L1: when I stop playing, the amp buzz should vanish instantly - total silence between my notes
tiers.L0: the drum sound from Phil Collins' 'In the Air Tonight' where the huge hit gets chopped off dead

tiers.L4: An upward expander: signals below threshold are boosted toward it with ratio 1:1 to 1:4, threshold -60 to 0 dB, attack and release controls; brings up low-level detail.
tiers.L3: an upward expander to bring out quiet details
tiers.L2: the opposite of squashing - it makes the quiet little details of my recording louder while leaving the loud parts alone
tiers.L1: surface the ghost notes and room air buried deep in my take - the stuff you feel more than hear
tiers.L0: what mastering engineers do to bring out the breaths and finger noise on a Norah Jones record

tiers.L4: A sidechain-capable compressor: stereo program input plus an external key input, threshold -60 to 0 dB, ratio up to 10:1, attack 0.1-50 ms, release 50-1000 ms; gain reduction driven by the key signal.
tiers.L3: a sidechain-capable compressor
tiers.L2: a compressor that ducks my track down whenever another sound like the kick drum hits, then lets it swell back up
tiers.L1: make my pads breathe in and out with the beat, dipping every time the kick lands
tiers.L0: the pumping sound of Eric Prydz's 'Call on Me'

tiers.L4: A sine-wave test oscillator: frequency 20 Hz-20 kHz with exponential taper defaulting to 440 Hz, amplitude 0-1 defaulting to 0.5; a pure sinusoid with no harmonics.
tiers.L3: a pure sine wave oscillator with frequency and amplitude
tiers.L2: a generator that plays one perfectly smooth, pure tone, with controls for its pitch and volume
tiers.L1: the cleanest possible beep - a single glassy tone with nothing rough or buzzy about it
tiers.L0: the 440 tuning tone, like the beep in a hearing test

tiers.L4: A sawtooth synth voice: band-limited sawtooth oscillator 40 Hz-4 kHz, ADSR amplitude envelope (attack 1-1000 ms, decay 1-1000 ms, sustain 0-1, release 10-3000 ms), and a gate control to trigger notes.
tiers.L3: a sawtooth synth with an ADSR envelope
tiers.L2: a buzzy synth tone whose volume shape I can control - how fast it starts, how it settles, and how long it takes to fade when I let go
tiers.L1: a bright sharp synth note that blooms open when I press and sighs away when I release
tiers.L0: the raw buzzing analog synth lead from 'Popcorn'

tiers.L4: A 2-operator FM synthesizer: sine carrier 40 Hz-2 kHz, modulator at an adjustable frequency ratio 0.25-8 of the carrier, modulation index 0-20; classic Chowning-style FM.
tiers.L3: a 2-operator FM synth with ratio and modulation index
tiers.L2: a synth where one tone wobbles another so fast it turns into bells and metallic timbres, with knobs for the flavor and the intensity
tiers.L1: glassy, bell-like electric tones - somewhere between a wine glass and a robot choir
tiers.L0: the DX7 electric-piano sound from every 80s ballad, like 'Careless Whisper'

tiers.L4: A white-noise generator with tone shaping: uniform white noise source into a one-pole low-pass tone control 100 Hz-15 kHz, plus an output level 0-1.
tiers.L3: a white noise generator with a tone control
tiers.L2: a static hiss generator with a knob that sweeps it from bright crackle down to a deep rumble
tiers.L1: the sound of ocean spray or a distant waterfall that I can brighten or darken
tiers.L0: the wind-and-surf sound from a white-noise sleep machine

tiers.L4: Karplus-Strong plucked-string synthesis: a noise-burst-excited delay line with a two-point averaging low-pass in the feedback loop, frequency 40 Hz-2 kHz, decay time and damping controls, and a trigger gate.
tiers.L3: a Karplus-Strong plucked string synthesizer
tiers.L2: an instrument that sounds like plucking a guitar string, with a pitch control and one for how long the note rings out
tiers.L1: a plucky harp-like note that dies away naturally, like touching a real string
tiers.L0: the plucked intro sound of The Police's 'Every Breath You Take', playable at different pitches
